title: School-board campaign money from these seven vendors or their staff, against the board’s items on their contracts
question: Did these vendors, or people who name them as employer, give to school-board candidates around the board’s items on the vendors’ contracts more often than the campaign calendar alone would give?
finding: Very little money, and no more inside the window than the calendar gives. 6,911 contributions since 2018 to 59 school-board candidate committees were checked; 9 contributions ($1,050) came from donors naming one of the seven vendors as employer, and none from a vendor itself. 6 fall within 180 days before to 365 days after a board item on that vendor, against 6.0 if they had been given on the same days as everyone else’s contributions to the same committees; 5 within 30 days, against 3.1. 1 of those inside the window went to a candidate who sat on the board at the item’s meeting. 9 contributions are too few to read as a pattern either way.
how: Candidate committees whose name contains "School Board" or "Board of Education", contributions (Schedule A) dated 2018 or later. A match is the employer an individual wrote, or an organisation’s name, equal after normalising to a spelling of one of the seven vendors (Robert Half counts for Protiviti, its parent; SAP Concur for SAP). The window is the one the timing screens use for City contracts (180 days before to 365 after). The expected count gives each matched contribution the share of all contributions to its committee that fall inside that vendor’s windows. Board seats come from Form 700 statements filed for the Board of Education.
limits: An employer entry is the donor’s own statement and a name match only: the records do not show whether the donor works for the vendor that contracts with the district. Board items here are only the seven vendors’ items saved in this pull, and the votes themselves are in minutes not on disk. Small contributions from staff of large employers are ordinary civic giving. Donors are not named.
